metaTitle: Do Cockroaches Bite? Rarely: What's Documented
metaDescription: Cockroaches can bite, but documented reports are few and the clearest involve extreme infestations. What is on record, likelier culprits and health risks.
h1: Do Cockroaches Bite? What Is Documented and What Probably Bit You Instead
dek: Cockroach bites are on record, but the reports are few. Here is what they describe, why a mark on your skin more likely has another cause, and the better documented health problems cockroaches cause.
excerpt: Cockroaches can bite, but the reports on record are few and the clearest describe extreme infestations. What is documented, what more likely bit you, and the real health risks.

quickAnswer.lead: **Yes, cockroaches can bite people, but documented bites are few, and the clearest reports describe extreme infestations.** [The University of Florida's German cockroach profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN128) says that in extremely heavy infestations the species has been reported to bite humans and to feed on food residues on the faces of sleeping people. For unexplained bites, the University of Kentucky's fact sheet lists bed bugs, fleas, lice and mites first.
bullets: A 1960 Smithsonian monograph says its authors had discussed about 20 reports of cockroaches biting people in a paper published in 1957.
The usual injury in those reports was abrasion of callused skin on the hands and feet, with small wounds sometimes left on the softer skin of the face and neck.
The same monograph cites five writers, from 1870 to 1943, who reported cockroaches so numerous on ships that they gnawed the skin and nails of the men on board.
The species named in the bite reports cited here are the German, American and Australian cockroaches.
One county health department says cockroaches do not bite but have heavy leg spines that may scratch.
In a study of 476 inner-city children with asthma, 36.8 percent were allergic to cockroach allergen and 50.2 percent of their bedrooms had high levels of it.

body.text: Do cockroaches bite people?

Yes, on occasion, and the clearest reports come from extreme infestations. [The University of Florida's profile of the German cockroach](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN128) says that in extremely heavy infestations the species has been reported to bite humans and to feed on food residues on the faces of sleeping people. That single sentence is as far as the profile goes. Biting is also not among the health risks in [the main reference on cockroach species, health effects and control](/learn/cockroaches), which centers on allergens, asthma and the microbes cockroaches carry onto food.

Not every authority agrees that cockroaches bite at all. [The St. Joseph County Department of Health in Indiana](https://www.in.gov/localhealth/stjosephcounty/environmental-health/healthy-homes/cockroaches/) states that they do not bite, and adds that their heavy leg spines may scratch. [The University of Kentucky's fact sheet on unexplained bites](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef649), written for people who believe they have a biting pest but have not identified the source, works through bed bugs, fleas, lice, mites, thrips, biting gnats and spiders and never mentions cockroaches.

Read together, the sources point the same way. A bite from a cockroach is possible and has been recorded, and it sits far down the list of explanations for a mark on your skin. None of these sources puts a figure on how often it happens, so calling cockroach bites rare is this page's reading of them and not a measured rate.
What is actually documented about cockroach bites?

The core of the record is about 20 reports, reviewed in a 1957 paper, that describe abrasions and small wounds. In [a 1960 Smithsonian monograph on cockroaches and the organisms they interact with](https://repository.si.edu/items/c9a92b90-dd0f-4cea-9e84-a872d59b87b5), Louis Roth and Edwin Willis wrote that cockroaches will on occasion attack and bite animals other than insects, and that a paper of theirs published in 1957 had discussed about 20 reports of cockroaches biting people. They summarized the injury as usually confined to abrasion of the callused parts of the hands and feet, with small wounds sometimes left in the softer skin of the face and neck.

The same monograph records bites aboard ships. Roth and Willis cite five writers, publishing between 1870 and 1943, who reported cockroaches so numerous on ships that they gnawed the skin and nails of the men on board. The authors call these independent observations of what may well have been a common occurrence on ships.

One more account, which the authors note they had left out of the 1957 paper, was published in 1924. Its author, Sonan, had his toes and chest nibbled by cockroaches while he slept on an island the monograph calls Hiyakejima. A policeman had already told him that American and Australian cockroaches (*Periplaneta americana* and *Periplaneta australasiae*) nibbled people there, and he had hardly believed it until it happened to him.

body.text: None of these sources puts a number on how often it happens. They give no rate, no count of recent cases and no number of roaches at which biting starts, and the University of Florida does not define an extremely heavy infestation. The reports Roth and Willis reviewed all date from 1957 or earlier, and the latest shipboard report they cite is from 1943. Against that record stands a county health department that says flatly that cockroaches do not bite.
Why would a cockroach bite a person?

The sources give no firm reason, but the details they record point to feeding and to sheer numbers. The University of Florida pairs biting with feeding on food residues on the faces of sleeping people, the injury Roth and Willis describe as usual is abrasion of callused skin, and the shipboard reports speak of gnawed skin and nails where roaches were very numerous. These passages describe nibbling and gnawing; none of them mentions blood feeding, a sting or venom. A common explanation, that roaches bite when a large population runs short of food, is not stated in any of the passages cited here.

Two details stand out. Both the Florida statement and the 1924 account involve sleeping people, and the Florida statement concerns extremely heavy infestations. The German cockroach is the species that statement names, and a separate guide covers [how to recognize German cockroaches and the bait program used against them](/blog/german-cockroaches).

Contact is not the same as a bite. A large roach that flies or drops onto you has not attacked you, and a separate guide covers [which cockroaches fly and why they sometimes head toward people](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly). A roach that runs across bare skin could also leave a mark without biting: the leg-spine scratch described by the St. Joseph County health department.

body.text: What does a cockroach bite look like?

It has no reliable look: none of the passages cited here gives a clinical picture that would let you tell a cockroach bite from any other small skin injury. The closest thing to a description is the Roth and Willis summary: abraded skin on callused parts of the hands and feet and, sometimes, small wounds on the softer skin of the face and neck. Descriptions that give a cockroach bite a particular size, color or pattern go beyond what these sources support.

The University of Kentucky is blunt about how little a mark can tell anyone. Its fact sheet says bug bites are difficult to diagnose, even by physicians. Writing about spiders, it adds that, as with other potential biters, a bite is extremely difficult to diagnose from the lesion alone, and that without an actual spider doing the biting such a diagnosis should be regarded as little more than a guess.

body.title: A mark is not an identification
body.text: The skin alone is a poor guide to what bit you. The useful evidence is the insect itself, caught or trapped where the marks are appearing.
What is more likely to have bitten you?

Bed bugs, fleas, lice and mites head the University of Kentucky's list of biting pests to consider, and some bite-like reactions are not caused by a pest at all. The table below summarizes how the fact sheet describes each one.

body.text: If you found a small brown insect near the bed and cannot tell whether it is a young cockroach or a bed bug, compare [what baby cockroaches look like beside bed bugs and beetles](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) with [what bed bugs look like at each life stage](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like).

Names add to the confusion. Oriental cockroaches are often called water bugs, a name that also belongs to a family of true bugs that live in water, so if that is the word you were given, see [how true water bugs differ from the cockroaches that share the name](/blog/water-bugs-vs-cockroaches).

body.text: How to find out what is biting
Work from evidence, not from the look of the mark. These steps follow the University of Kentucky's approach to unexplained bites.

items: Ask whether anyone has actually seen or caught an insect while the irritation was happening; the fact sheet calls this one of the most important questions.
Note how many people are affected and where in the building it happens, because a pattern narrows the list.

Set several glue traps in the places where bites have been reported. The fact sheet cautions that such traps are not always reliable, but they can help show whether a biting pest is present. The same kind of trap is also used to detect cockroaches, as a related guide on [how glue traps find roaches and bait stations kill them](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada) explains.
Save anything you catch in a non-crushable container, not in an envelope or under tape, so it can be identified.
If no biting pest turns up, see a dermatologist; the fact sheet says a person in that position should be referred to a dermatologist, an industrial hygienist or another allied professional.

body.text: What should you do about a suspected cockroach bite?

Treat it like any minor insect bite: clean it, ease the itch and watch it for a few days. [The MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, on the National Library of Medicine's consumer health site](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000033.htm), says that in most cases bites and stings can be easily treated at home. Its general first aid steps include the four below; follow the label directions on any medicine you use.

items: Wash the site thoroughly with soap and water.
Place ice wrapped in a washcloth on the site for 10 minutes, take it off for 10 minutes, and repeat.
If necessary, take an antihistamine or apply a cream that reduces itching.
Over the next several days, watch for signs of infection such as increasing redness, swelling or pain.

body.title: When to get medical help
body.text: Call 911 for trouble breathing, wheezing, swelling anywhere on the face or in the mouth, throat tightness, difficulty swallowing, feeling weak or turning blue. MedlinePlus lists these as reasons to call 911 for someone with a sting, and it says severe, life-threatening allergic reactions can follow insect bites as well as bee stings. Contact a healthcare provider if a mark shows signs of infection, if new marks keep appearing, or if you cannot find the cause.
What are the real health risks from cockroaches?
Allergy and asthma are the risks stated most firmly, followed by contamination of food. Both happen without a cockroach ever touching you.
Allergens and asthma

The clearest numbers come from [a study of 476 inner-city children with asthma, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9134876/). The children were 4 to 9 years old and lived in eight inner-city areas of the United States. Researchers skin-tested each child for allergy to cockroach, dust-mite and cat allergens and measured those allergens in household dust.

head: Allergen
Children allergic to it
Bedrooms with high levels
body.caption: Rosenstreich and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 1997; 476 children with asthma in eight US inner-city areas. High levels were defined by proposed thresholds for causing disease.

body.text: After the researchers adjusted for sex, a behavior checklist score and family history of asthma, children who were both allergic to cockroach allergen and exposed to high levels of it had 0.37 hospitalizations a year, compared with 0.11 for the other children, and 2.56 unscheduled medical visits for asthma a year, compared with 1.43. They also had significantly more days of wheezing, missed school days and nights of lost sleep. Similar patterns were not found for dust-mite or cat allergen. The authors worded their conclusion carefully: the combination may help explain how often inner-city children have asthma-related health problems.

The University of Florida profile adds that German cockroaches may cause severe allergic responses, and the St. Joseph County health department says the cockroach is considered an allergen source and an asthma trigger for residents. If anyone in the home has asthma or allergy symptoms that are worse indoors, tell their healthcare provider about the cockroaches.
Germs carried on and in the body

Cockroaches carry disease organisms, though evidence tying them to specific outbreaks is thin. The University of Florida says German cockroaches physically transport and often harbor pathogenic organisms, and that they adulterate food and food products with their feces and defensive secretions. The St. Joseph County health department adds the caveat that little evidence exists to link the cockroach to specific disease outbreaks. A cautious reading is to treat food, dishes and counters that roaches have crossed as contaminated, without assuming that a sighting means someone will get sick.
Stress and stigma

The Florida profile also notes that some scientists suggest German cockroach infestations may cause psychological stress, and that the stigma attached to an infestation changes how people behave. The St. Joseph County health department likewise says the sight of cockroaches can cause considerable psychological or emotional distress in some people. That is one more reason to deal with the infestation itself and not only the mark on your skin.
How do you keep cockroaches from biting or crawling on you?

Reduce the number of cockroaches, because the one condition the University of Florida attaches to biting is an extremely heavy infestation. Since the same sentence mentions food residues on the faces of sleeping people, washing your face and hands before bed and keeping food out of the bedroom are reasonable precautions. No source cited here has tested whether they change anything.

The lasting fix is to clear the infestation. [A step-by-step, bait-first plan for clearing cockroaches](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada) covers the method, and [the routes cockroaches use to get into a home and how to close each one](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from) covers keeping new ones out.

If roaches are reaching the bed at night, bringing in a professional is reasonable; see [what professional pest control typically costs](/blog/how-much-is-pest-control) before you request quotes. If the marks continue after the roaches are gone, go back to the list of other causes above and to a healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Do cockroaches bite people in their sleep?
faqs.answer: Two of the accounts behind this page involve sleeping people. The University of Florida says that in extremely heavy infestations German cockroaches have been reported to bite humans and to feed on food residues on the faces of sleeping people, and a 1924 account retold in a Smithsonian monograph describes a man whose toes and chest were nibbled while he slept. Documented reports like these are few. For bites that appear overnight, look for bed bugs first: the University of Kentucky says bed bugs should always be considered when bites are unexplained, that people are usually bitten at night while they are sleeping, and that the bite is painless at first.

faqs.question: Which cockroaches bite?
faqs.answer: Three species are named in the bite reports summarized on this page. The University of Florida's statement concerns the German cockroach, and a 1924 account retold by Roth and Willis in a Smithsonian monograph names the American and Australian cockroaches. The sentence in which the same authors cite shipboard reports names no species. None of these passages says that any species bites habitually or seeks people out. The condition attached to the Florida statement is the size of the infestation, described as extremely heavy, not the kind of cockroach.

faqs.question: Can a cockroach scratch you?
faqs.answer: Possibly. The St. Joseph County Department of Health in Indiana says cockroaches do not bite but have heavy leg spines that may scratch. None of the other passages cited on this page mentions scratching, and the department gives no detail on how often it happens or what the scratch looks like. If a roach has run across your skin and left broken skin behind, wash the spot with soap and water and watch it over the next several days for increasing redness, swelling or pain.

faqs.question: Are cockroach bites dangerous?
faqs.answer: The injuries described in the reports summarized here are small. Roth and Willis summarized them as abrasion of callused skin on the hands and feet and, sometimes, small wounds on the softer skin of the face and neck. None of the passages cited on this page links a cockroach bite to a specific disease. MedlinePlus advises washing a bite with soap and water and watching for signs of infection, such as increasing redness, swelling or pain, over the next several days. The better documented health problem from cockroaches is allergy and asthma.

faqs.question: Should I see a doctor for a suspected cockroach bite?
faqs.answer: Contact a healthcare provider if the mark shows signs of infection such as increasing redness, swelling or pain, if new marks keep appearing, or if you cannot find the cause. The University of Kentucky notes that bug bites are difficult to diagnose even by physicians and recommends keeping specimens in non-crushable containers, and MedlinePlus says to bring the insect that bit you, if possible, so it can be identified. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or mouth, throat tightness, feeling weak or turning blue, which MedlinePlus lists as reasons to call for someone with a sting.

faqs.question: Can cockroaches make you sick without biting you?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is the better documented concern. In a 1997 New England Journal of Medicine study of 476 inner-city children with asthma, 36.8 percent were allergic to cockroach allergen and 50.2 percent of bedrooms had high levels of it. Children who were both allergic and highly exposed had 0.37 hospitalizations a year, compared with 0.11 for the others. The University of Florida also says German cockroaches physically transport and often harbor pathogenic organisms and adulterate food with their feces and secretions.
